newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's premier Kengo thrives among enemies.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's premier Kengo thrives among enemies.

text.p: Kengo wa Dondo has many political enemies and lacks mass appeal but he again emerged as the compromise choice for Zaire's prime minsiter in a bitterly divided field.
President Mobutu Sese Seko on Tuesday issued a decree naming Kengo as the head of a new crisis cabinet to guide the war effort to retake land from ethnic Tutsi rebels in eastern Zaire.
Kengo had several cards in his hand, notably his popularity among Western donors and the laws laid out by Zaire's transitional constitution.
His supporters argued that removing the incumbent prime minister without resort to a lengthy parliamentary procedure would be unconstitutional.
But the same constitution is also a crucial factor preventing Kengo's career from rising any further.
His mixed-race parentage prevents him legally from taking part in presidential elections due next year, while assuring that he could never be a threat to Mobutu's own position.
Local commentators say this fact, and the support he has won among Western donors in the past two years for his attempts to reform Zaire's corrupt economy, have made him useful to Mobutu.
Born in 1934, Kengo's father was a Polish Jew naturalised as a Belgian. His mother is said to have been half Tutsi and half Ngbandi, the tribe of Mobutu's Equateur region Kengo grew up in.

Recently Kengo's many enemies have exploited his part-Tutsi origins to promote popular hatred of the premier. They argue he is not Zairean and so unqualified to lead the country in the war against ethnic Tutsi rebels said by Kinshasa to be backed by Tutsi-led armies in neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi.

Kengo served under Mobutu on numerous occasions in Zaire's turbulent post-independence history. He was prime minister in 1982-86 and again from 1988 to 1990, before the transition from one-party rule.

He came back to the top of the government in 1994 when he was elected by a newly installed majority in the transitional parliament. He was said at the time to have been a consensus candidate who, unlike Mobutu's radical opponent Etienne Tshisekedi, could work with Zaire's all-powerful ruler.

His post is still bitterly contested by Tshisekedi, who since being shunted aside in favour of a Mobutu appointee in 1993 has claimed to be the only legitimate prime minister elected by a sovereign national conference.

Kengo also has many enemies in the president's entourage, especially among those who profited from the country's diamond trade. They were financially damaged in 1994 when Kengo expelled members of the Lebanese community who he accused of oiling the motor of the illicit trade.
Kengo himself is reputed to have enormous wealth.
As well as his official residence he has a huge private house in a wealthy district of the otherwise crumbling capital, and a neo-classical palace under construction nearby.
Personal friends, however, skirt over his long career as a member of Mobutu's one-party regime and say that he is a rigorous man of the law true to his education and early training as a lawyer.
"He is the prototype of a jurist, rigorous and obedient to the text," said one close ally, who added that he played tennis almost every morning.
Married with children, Kengo is also a practicising Roman Catholic and has been reported to read the Bible while travelling by plane.
